title: Likelihood Theory & Estimation Mechanics
text:
Last week we built a model for a binary \(y\) from the ground up. We looked at \(y\), wrote down the probability distribution that described it, took the joint probability of the whole sample, logged it, made the distribution’s parameter a function of \(x\beta\), and chose a link function \(F\) to map the linear prediction on the appropriate (probability) space. Six steps, and at the end of them we were holding a log-likelihood function:
\[
\ell(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big[\, y_i \log \pi_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-\pi_i)\,\big],
\qquad \pi_i = F(x_i\beta).
\]
Then we used glm to estimate the logit and generated quantities of interest.
What we haven’t covered is how the model got estimated — what goes on in the magic box when we call glm with a binomial family and a logit link. Filling that gap is the task here, answering these questions:

What is a likelihood, and how does it differ from a probability?
Given data and a log-likelihood, how do we solve for the unknowns — and what, dimensionally, are we solving?
Why are some estimates precise with small standard errors and others are not, and how does that arise from the data and the math of likelihood?

This will illustrate something we mentioned last week. In interpretation, a nonlinear model differs from a linear one in exactly one respect: we transform the linear prediction by \(F\). In estimation, the two technologies are genuinely different. OLS gives you a single formula to apply to the data. Maximum likelihood, in almost every case we care about, does not — it builds a formula out of the data, then tries different “models,” comparing them until it finds the one most likely to have generated what we observed.

title: Likelihood Theory & Estimation Mechanics
text:
The binomial log-likelihood, written out
Make it concrete with the binomial, the model from last week. For a single binary outcome \(y_i\), write \(\pi_i = Pr(y_i = 1)\) for the probability of a one. The density of one observation is the Bernoulli, and we map the linear predictor \(x_i\beta\) into that probability with a link function \(F\):
\[
f(y_i \mid \pi_i) = \pi_i^{y_i}(1-\pi_i)^{1-y_i},
\qquad
\pi_i = F(x_i\beta).
\]
Take the log of that density, sum over the \(n\) observations, and substitute the link for \(\pi_i\). That gives us the form we will use for the rest of the semester:
\[
\ell(\beta) \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[\;
\underbrace{y_i \log F(x_i\beta)}_{\text{the ones}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{(1-y_i)\log\big(1 - F(x_i\beta)\big)}_{\text{the zeros}}
\;\Big]
\]
Read it as two mirror-image parts, because that’s what it is. The \(y_i\) out front of the first term and the \((1-y_i)\) out front of the second are doing switching work: when \(y_i = 1\) the second term is multiplied by zero and vanishes, and when \(y_i = 0\) the first term vanishes. So every observation in the sample contributes exactly one of the two, never both. The ones contribute \(\log Pr(y_i = 1)\), and the zeros contribute \(\log Pr(y_i = 0)\).
That reading tells you what maximizing this thing actually does. We are looking for the \(\beta\) that simultaneously pushes \(F(x_i\beta)\) up toward one at every row where we observed a dispute, and pushes it down toward zero at every row where we didn’t. Those two demands pull in opposite directions — the same coefficient has to serve both — and \(\widehat\beta\) is the best available compromise between them. When we say maximum likelihood “makes the observed data as probable as possible,” this is the arithmetic of that sentence.
Now notice where the link sits. \(F\) appears in both halves and nowhere else. Everything that distinguishes one binary model from another lives inside those two \(F\)’s, which is why swapping the link is the whole difference between a logit and a probit. Written out:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{logit:}\quad
\ell(\beta) &= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[\, y_i \log \Lambda(x_i\beta) + (1-y_i)\log\big(1-\Lambda(x_i\beta)\big)\,\Big],
&& \Lambda(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}} \\[6pt]
\text{probit:}\quad
\ell(\beta) &= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[\, y_i \log \Phi(x_i\beta) + (1-y_i)\log\big(1-\Phi(x_i\beta)\big)\,\Big],
&& \Phi(z) = \int_{-\infty}^{z}\phi(u)\,du
\end{aligned}
\]
Same structure, same two parts, one substitution. Hold onto that; when we get to counts and durations we will write down log-likelihoods that look nothing like these, and the thing that stays constant is the procedure, not the formula.






An aside: the logit’s compact form, and why the coefficients are log-odds



For the logit specifically — and only the logit — the two parts can be regrouped into something more compact. Distribute the \((1-y_i)\), gather the two \(y_i\) terms into a single log of a ratio, and that ratio \(\pi_i/(1-\pi_i)\) is the odds that \(y_i = 1\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell(\beta)
&= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big[\, y_i \log \pi_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-\pi_i)\,\big] \\[4pt]
&= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big[\, y_i \log \pi_i - y_i \log(1-\pi_i) + \log(1-\pi_i)\,\big] \\[4pt]
&= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[\, y_i \log\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i} + \log(1-\pi_i)\,\Big] \\[4pt]
&= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big[\, y_i\, x_i\beta - \log\!\big(1 + e^{x_i\beta}\big)\,\big].
\end{aligned}
\]
The last step is where the logit earns its keep: the logit link sets the log-odds equal to the linear predictor, \(\log[\pi_i/(1-\pi_i)] = x_i\beta\), exactly — which is the fact behind the odds-ratio interpretation we used last week. And since \(\pi_i = 1/(1+e^{-x_i\beta})\), rearranging gives \(1-\pi_i = 1/(1+e^{x_i\beta})\), so \(\log(1-\pi_i) = -\log(1+e^{x_i\beta})\).
It’s worth seeing once, because you will meet it in textbooks and because it explains the log-odds scale. But don’t take it as the general form — it is a logit-only convenience. The probit has no such regrouping; \(\Phi\) doesn’t oblige. The two-part version above is the one that generalizes, so that’s the one we’ll write.

title: Likelihood Theory & Estimation Mechanics
text:
Where the algebra works
Take the binomial with no \(x\) variables at all. Every observation shares the same probability \(\pi\) — there is one unknown, a single number, and we want the value of it that makes our observed string of zeros and ones most probable. Write the log-likelihood, differentiate with respect to \(\pi\), set it to zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell(\pi) &= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big[\, y_i\log\pi + (1-y_i)\log(1-\pi)\,\big] \\[4pt]
          &= \Big(\textstyle\sum_i y_i\Big)\log\pi \;+\; \Big(n - \textstyle\sum_i y_i\Big)\log(1-\pi) \\[4pt]
\frac{d\ell}{d\pi} &= \frac{\sum_i y_i}{\pi} \;-\; \frac{n - \sum_i y_i}{1-\pi} \;=\; 0 \\[4pt]
(1-\pi)\textstyle\sum_i y_i &= \pi\Big(n - \textstyle\sum_i y_i\Big) \\[4pt]
\textstyle\sum_i y_i &= \pi\, n \\[4pt]
\widehat\pi &= \bbox[#A7DA92, 3pt, border: 1px solid #005A43]{\;\frac{\sum_i y_i}{n} \;=\; \bar y\;}
\end{aligned}
\]
The second line just counts: \(\sum_i y_i\) observations contribute a \(\log\pi\), the remaining \(n - \sum_i y_i\) contribute a \(\log(1-\pi)\). Two steps of algebra from there, and the answer is the sample mean of \(y\). No software, no starting value, no algorithm — a formula.
On the dispute data, that formula says the maximum likelihood estimate of \(\pi\) is the observed dispute rate:


code
dp <- read_dta(here::here("data", "dp.dta"))
dp$lncaprat <- log(dp$caprat)   # a capability ratio is multiplicative, so model it on the log scale

round(mean(dp$dispute), 4)


[1] 0.0451


Now the same thing with a different distribution, to show this isn’t a peculiarity of the binomial. Suppose \(y\) is a count — Snickers bars without peanuts produced in an 8 hour shift — so the Poisson, whose parameter \(\lambda\) is the rate at which events occur. Density, log-likelihood, derivative:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(y_i \mid \lambda) &= \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{y_i}}{y_i!} \\[4pt]
\ell(\lambda) &= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big[\, -\lambda + y_i\log\lambda - \log(y_i!)\,\big] \\[4pt]
              &= -n\lambda \;+\; \Big(\textstyle\sum_i y_i\Big)\log\lambda \;-\; \textstyle\sum_i \log(y_i!) \\[4pt]
\frac{d\ell}{d\lambda} &= -n + \frac{\sum_i y_i}{\lambda} \;=\; 0 \\[4pt]
\widehat\lambda &= \bbox[#A7DA92, 3pt, border: 1px solid #005A43]{\;\frac{\sum_i y_i}{n} \;=\; \bar y\;}
\end{aligned}
\]
Again a formula, again the sample mean. Note the \(\log(y_i!)\) term: no \(\lambda\) in it, so it vanishes on differentiation. It is part of the likelihood’s magnitude, and magnitude carries no information.
Try it on a small set of real counts. Here are Snickers bars without peanuts produced in an 8 hour shift, one count per shift:
\[
y = \{5,\; 0,\; 1,\; 1,\; 0,\; 3,\; 2,\; 3,\; 4,\; 1\}
\]
That first shift doesn’t like peanuts.


code
cw <- c(5, 0, 1, 1, 0, 3, 2, 3, 4, 1)

c(sum_y      = sum(cw),
  n          = length(cw),
  lambda_hat = sum(cw) / length(cw),
  glm_check  = unname(exp(coef(glm(cw ~ 1, family = poisson)))))


     sum_y          n lambda_hat  glm_check 
        20         10          2          2 


\(\widehat\lambda = 20/10 = 2\), and a Poisson glm with nothing but a constant agrees exactly.
So: two different distributions, two different parameters, the same procedure — write \(\ell\), differentiate, set to zero, solve — and a closed-form answer both times.2 Figure 3 draws both log-likelihoods, with the closed-form answer marked on each.


code
# Two distributions, two parameters, the same shape of problem. Each curve is
# the log-likelihood over its one unknown; each dashed line is the value the
# algebra produced. I plot RELATIVE log-likelihood (subtracting the maximum) so
# the two panels are comparable -- remember the level carries no information.

pi_hat  <- mean(dp$dispute)
g_pi    <- seq(0.030, 0.070, length.out = 400)
ll_pi   <- sum(dp$dispute) * log(g_pi) + sum(1 - dp$dispute) * log(1 - g_pi)

p_bern <- ggplot(tibble(pi = g_pi, rel = ll_pi - max(ll_pi)), aes(pi, rel)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = bu_green) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = pi_hat, linetype = "dashed", color = bu_black) +
  annotate("text", x = pi_hat, y = -95, hjust = -0.1, size = 3.6, color = bu_black,
           label = paste0("hat(pi) == ", round(pi_hat, 4)), parse = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "Bernoulli: militarized disputes",
       subtitle = expression(hat(pi) == bar(y) ~ ", the sample proportion"),
       x = expression(pi), y = "relative log-likelihood") +
  theme_minimal()

lam_hat <- mean(cw)
g_lam   <- seq(0.6, 4.2, length.out = 400)
ll_lam  <- -length(cw) * g_lam + sum(cw) * log(g_lam) - sum(lfactorial(cw))

p_pois <- ggplot(tibble(lambda = g_lam, rel = ll_lam - max(ll_lam)), aes(lambda, rel)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = bu_lightgreen) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = lam_hat, linetype = "dashed", color = bu_black) +
  annotate("text", x = lam_hat, y = -7.5, hjust = -0.1, size = 3.6, color = bu_black,
           label = paste0("hat(lambda) == ", lam_hat), parse = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "Poisson: civil wars in Africa",
       subtitle = expression(hat(lambda) == sum(y[i]) / n ~ ", also a sample mean"),
       x = expression(lambda), y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

p_bern + p_pois








Figure 3





Two things about that figure. The shapes are the same — one smooth hill with one top — which is the structural fact that makes the calculus work in both cases. But the widths are wildly different, and that isn’t cosmetic: nearly 21,000 dyad-years on the left, ten Snickers shifts on the right. Hold that thought; by the end of these notes the width of the hill at the top will be the standard error.
If maximum likelihood always went like this, it would be a footnote in a calculus course rather than a semester-long class.

title: Likelihood Theory & Estimation Mechanics
text:
Where the algebra stops
Here is the catch, and it is not where you might expect.
We don’t actually want a single \(\pi\) or a single \(\lambda\) for the whole sample. We want them to vary with covariates — that’s the entire point of a regression. So we parameterize: we make the distribution’s parameter a function of \(x\beta\), which is step 5 of last week’s build. For the Poisson, \(\lambda_i = \exp(x_i\beta)\), the exponential keeping the rate positive. Substitute and differentiate again, this time with respect to \(\beta\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell(\beta) &= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big[\, -e^{x_i\beta} + y_i\, x_i\beta - \log(y_i!)\,\big] \\[4pt]
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \beta} &= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(y_i - e^{x_i\beta}\big)\,x_i' \;=\; X'(y - \lambda) \;=\; 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]
The derivative came out fine. It is clean, it is interpretable, and we can compute it for any \(\beta\) we like. What we cannot do is solve it. Try to isolate \(\beta\): it is stuck inside \(e^{x_i\beta}\), wrapped up with the data, and no rearranging gets it out by itself.
The binomial does the same thing. From the log-likelihood we derived above, the derivative with respect to \(\beta\) works out to
\[
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \beta} \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \pi_i)\,x_i' \;=\; X'(y - \pi) \;=\; 0,
\qquad \pi_i = \Lambda(x_i\beta),
\]
and again \(\beta\) is buried — this time inside \(\Lambda\).
Now set that beside the least-squares problem. Minimizing the sum of squared residuals gives the normal equations,
\[
X'(y - X\beta) \;=\; 0,
\]
which look almost identical. Almost. The difference is that here \(\beta\) appears linearly, out in the open and multiplied by a matrix we know, so one line of algebra finishes the job: \(X'y = X'X\beta\), therefore \(\widehat\beta = (X'X)^{-1}X'y\).






The one difference that matters



Maximum likelihood does not fail at differentiation. It fails at inversion. We can always write the derivative; what we usually cannot do is solve it for \(\beta\), because \(\beta\) sits inside a nonlinear function. That single fact is why OLS finishes in one line and maximum likelihood has to climb a hill.


That difference is visible if we simply plot the two derivatives. Both problems are the same task — find the value of \(\beta\) where the derivative crosses zero. Figure 4 shows what we have to work with in each case.


code
# Same job in both panels: find where the derivative crosses zero. On the left
# the derivative is a straight line, so we can solve for the crossing. On the
# right it is a curve, so we cannot -- we have to hunt for it. I sweep the
# coefficient on lncaprat, holding each model's intercept at its own estimate.
# (The vertical scales differ; the shapes are the point, not the levels.)

xv <- dp$lncaprat; yv <- dp$dispute
a_ols   <- coef(lm(yv ~ xv))[1]
a_logit <- coef(glm(yv ~ xv, family = binomial))[1]
g_b <- seq(-0.60, 0.20, length.out = 300)

d_ols <- tibble(b = g_b, s = sapply(g_b, \(b) sum(xv * (yv - a_ols - xv * b))))
d_log <- tibble(b = g_b, s = sapply(g_b, \(b) sum(xv * (yv - plogis(a_logit + xv * b)))))

root_ols <- coef(lm(yv ~ xv))[2]
root_log <- coef(glm(yv ~ xv, family = binomial))[2]

p_ols <- ggplot(d_ols, aes(b, s)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = bu_grey) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = bu_green) +
  geom_point(x = root_ols, y = 0, size = 3, color = bu_black) +
  labs(title = "OLS: the derivative is a straight line",
       subtitle = expression(X*minute*(y - X*beta) ~ ": " ~ beta ~ "appears linearly, so we can solve"),
       x = expression("coefficient on lncaprat," ~ beta), y = "derivative") +
  theme_minimal()

p_log <- ggplot(d_log, aes(b, s)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = bu_grey) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = bu_lightgreen) +
  geom_point(x = root_log, y = 0, size = 3, color = bu_black) +
  labs(title = "Logit: the derivative is a curve",
       subtitle = expression(X*minute*(y - Lambda(X*beta)) ~ ": " ~ beta ~ "is inside" ~ Lambda ~ ", so we cannot"),
       x = expression("coefficient on lncaprat," ~ beta), y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

p_ols + p_log








Figure 4





Both curves cross zero exactly once, and in both cases that crossing is the estimate we want — the black dot. The difference is entirely in the shape. A straight line has an equation you can rearrange: two points determine it, and you can solve for its root in one step. The logit’s derivative bends, and it bends because \(\beta\) is trapped inside \(\Lambda\); there is no rearranging that produces “$= $ something.” The root is sitting right there in the picture, plainly visible, and we still have no formula for it.
That is the whole of the difference between the two technologies, and it is why the rest of this course spends so much time on searching. Since we cannot solve for \(\beta\) directly, we search for it: guess a \(\beta\), evaluate the derivative, use what it tells us to make a better guess, and repeat until the derivative is essentially zero. That is the rest of these notes and all of next week’s.
The matrix-algebra version of this same argument — the score equations set against the OLS normal equations, step for step — is written out in the MLE estimator notes. Read that alongside this file; it does the derivation without code, the way the OLS variance notes do for the linear model.

title: Likelihood Theory & Estimation Mechanics
section: The same machine, in the case you already know
text:
The same machine, in the case you already know
Before we go hill-climbing, run the identical recipe on one more distribution. Suppose \(y\) is continuous and we call it Normal, \(y \sim N(x\beta, \sigma^2)\) — conditional mean the linear predictor, variance constant across observations. Density, log, sum, differentiate with respect to \(\beta\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell(\beta,\sigma^2) &= -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2)
   \;-\; \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(y - X\beta)'(y - X\beta) \\[4pt]
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \beta} &= \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\,X'(y - X\beta) \;=\; 0 \\[4pt]
X'y &= X'X\beta \\[4pt]
\widehat\beta &= (X'X)^{-1}X'y .
\end{aligned}
\]
Two things. Only the last term of \(\ell\) involves \(\beta\), so the term carrying \(\sigma^2\) and the \(2\pi\) drops out on differentiation; and \(\sigma^2\) then divides out entirely when we set the derivative to zero, which is why \(\widehat\beta\) doesn’t depend on it.
And the answer is the OLS estimator, exactly. OLS is the maximum likelihood estimator for the linear model. The technology doesn’t compete with least squares or replace it; it contains it, as the special case where the outcome is Normal.
Notice the shape of the derivative in all three cases. Normal: \(X'(y - X\beta)\). Binomial: \(X'(y - \pi)\). Poisson: \(X'(y - \lambda)\). Every one is \(X'(\,y - \text{fitted}\,)\) — the design matrix times the gap between what we observed and what the model predicts. Three distributions, three links, one shape: the claim from Section 2.1 arriving on schedule.






Take away




Writing down a log-likelihood and solving it are two different jobs. The first recipe always works the same way; the second one is where models differ in difficulty.
With no covariates, calculus finishes the job — differentiate, set to zero, solve. We did it twice, for two different distributions, and both answers were a sample mean.
Add covariates and it stops working. \(\beta\) ends up buried inside a nonlinear function — \(e^{x\beta}\), \(\Lambda(x\beta)\) — and no rearranging gets it out.
OLS is the exception, and it is worth knowing exactly why: \(\beta\) sits out in the open, multiplied by a matrix we already know. That is also why OLS is the maximum likelihood estimator for the linear model — the technology contains least squares rather than competing with it.
Every one of these derivatives has the same shape, \(X'(y - \text{fitted})\). The link decides what “fitted” means; the machine around it does not change.

title: Likelihood Theory & Estimation Mechanics
text:
The binomial log-likelihood
Make it concrete with the binomial. For a single binary outcome \(y_i\), write \(\pi_i = Pr(y_i = 1)\) for the probability of a one. The density of one observation is the Bernoulli, and we map the linear predictor \(x_i\beta\) into that probability with a link function \(F\):
\[
f(y_i \mid \pi_i) = \pi_i^{y_i}(1-\pi_i)^{1-y_i},
\qquad
\pi_i = F(x_i\beta).
\]
Those two objects are the two green boxes from the machine, in that order. The quantity we want is \(\pi_i\), a probability. The Bernoulli \(f(y_i \mid \pi_i)\) is the first box, and looking at \(y\) all but picks it: the outcome is a zero or a one. The link \(F\) is the second box and a separate decision — \(\pi_i\) must land in \([0,1]\) and \(x_i\beta\) has no such manners, it will happily return \(-4.2\) or \(17\). Any well-behaved CDF would discipline it; which one we pick is a separate argument, and one we have already had.
Those are the only two substantive choices in the model. Everything downstream — forming \(X\beta\), summing logs, differentiating, inverting, taking square roots — is machinery that neither knows nor cares that the outcome is binary. Build the Poisson in a few weeks and we change exactly these two lines, then run the identical remainder.
Take the log of that density, sum over the \(n\) observations, and substitute the link for \(\pi_i\). That gives us the form we will use for the rest of the semester:
\[
\ell(\beta) \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[\;
\underbrace{y_i \log F(x_i\beta)}_{\text{the ones}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{(1-y_i)\log\big(1 - F(x_i\beta)\big)}_{\text{the zeros}}
\;\Big]
\]
As we discussed last week, the two parts of this log-likelihood are mirror images, corresponding to the structure of a binary variable. The \(y_i\) out front of the first term and the \((1-y_i)\) out front of the second are doing switching work: when \(y_i = 1\) the second term is multiplied by zero and vanishes, and when \(y_i = 0\) the first term vanishes. So every observation in the sample contributes exactly one of the two, never both. The ones contribute \(\log Pr(y_i = 1)\), and the zeros contribute \(\log Pr(y_i = 0)\).

title: Likelihood Theory & Estimation Mechanics
section: Why the math approach doesn’t work
text:
Why the math approach doesn’t work
Here is the thing — we don’t want a single \(\pi\) or a single \(\lambda\) for the whole sample. We want them to vary with covariates; that’s the point of the regression. So we parameterize: for the Poisson, \(\lambda_i = \exp(x_i\beta)\), the exponential keeping the rate positive. Substitute and differentiate with respect to \(\beta\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell(\beta) &= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big[\, -e^{x_i\beta} + y_i\, x_i\beta - \log(y_i!)\,\big] \\[4pt]
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \beta} &= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(y_i - e^{x_i\beta}\big)\,x_i' \;=\; X'(y - \lambda) \;=\; 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]
The derivative came out fine — clean, interpretable, computable for any \(\beta\) we like. What we cannot do is solve it. Try to isolate \(\beta\): it is stuck inside \(e^{x_i\beta}\), wrapped up with the data, and no rearranging gets it out.
The binomial does the same thing. From the log-likelihood we derived above, the derivative with respect to \(\beta\) works out to
\[
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \beta} \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \pi_i)\,x_i' \;=\; X'(y - \pi) \;=\; 0,
\qquad \pi_i = \Lambda(x_i\beta),
\]
and again \(\beta\) is buried — this time inside \(\Lambda\).
Compare that to the least-squares problem. Minimizing the sum of squared residuals gives the normal equations,
\[
X'(y - X\beta) \;=\; 0,
\]
which look almost identical. Almost. The difference is that here \(\beta\) appears linearly, out in the open and multiplied by a matrix we know, so one line of algebra finishes the job: \(X'y = X'X\beta\), therefore \(\widehat\beta = (X'X)^{-1}X'y\).
That is the whole of the difference between the two technologies, and it is why the rest of this course spends so much time on searching. Since we cannot solve for \(\beta\) directly, we search for it: guess a \(\beta\), evaluate the derivative, use what it tells us to make a better guess, and repeat until the derivative is essentially zero. That is the rest of these notes and all of the maximization notes.

title: Likelihood Theory & Estimation Mechanics
Likelihood Theory & Estimation Mechanics
section: The score: what the model is still getting wrong
text:
The score: what the model is still getting wrong
The first derivative of the log-likelihood goes by two names we use interchangeably — the score, or the gradient — written \(\nabla\ell(\beta)\) either way.
Start with what it is. The log-likelihood assigns one number to every candidate \(\beta\): how probable this sample is under it. The score asks a question about that number, one coefficient at a time — nudge this coefficient up a hair, holding the others still; does the sample get more probable or less? One answer per coefficient, so the score is a \(k \times 1\) vector. Positive says raise it, negative says lower it, and when every entry is zero at once — no nudge to anything helps — we are on top of the hill.
For the logit the score takes an unusually clean form:
\[
\nabla\ell(\beta) \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \pi_i)\,x_i' \;=\; X'(y - \pi).
\]
Read it in words. \((y - \pi)\) is the model’s mistakes, one per row; multiplying by \(X'\) runs each covariate’s column against those mistakes and sums, one number per covariate. So:

each element of the score is the leftover association between one covariate and what the model is currently getting wrong.

Say the model systematically under-predicts disputes in bordering dyads. Then the mistakes are positive in exactly the rows where border is 1, their products are positive, and the border score comes out positive: this coefficient is too small, and that column still has unused information in it.
Read the maximum the same way. Setting \(\nabla\ell(\beta) = 0\) says there is no leftover association between any covariate and the mistakes — every column of \(X\) used up. Which is the condition OLS imposes when it makes residuals orthogonal to regressors, \(X'e = 0\), with \(\pi\) playing the part \(X\beta\) plays there. Same machine, again.
The actual numbers, on the ten-row slice, starting from \(\beta = 0\):


code
# Evaluate the score at beta = 0, on the ten-row slice from above. With every
# coefficient at zero the linear prediction is zero for every row, so every
# fitted probability is Lambda(0) = .5 and every mistake is +/- 0.5.
b0 <- rep(0, ncol(X))
pi <- plogis(as.vector(X %*% b0))      # all 0.5

# The score multiplies each column of X against those mistakes and sums: one
# number per coefficient.
sc <- as.vector(t(X) %*% (y - pi))
names(sc) <- colnames(X)

round(y - pi, 3)                 # the mistakes, one per row (n x 1)


 [1]  0.5  0.5  0.5  0.5 -0.5 -0.5 -0.5 -0.5 -0.5 -0.5


code
round(sc, 3)                     # the score, one per coefficient (k x 1)


(Intercept)    lncaprat      border        deml 
     -1.000      -8.702       1.000      -3.000 


At \(\beta = 0\) every row gets even odds, so the mistakes are all \(\pm 0.5\): positive for the four disputes the model under-predicted, negative for the six non-disputes it over-predicted. Now read the four entries of the score, each one a verdict on a coefficient.

The constant’s column is all ones, so its score is just the ten mistakes added up: -1. Six negatives and four positives, so the intercept wants to come down a little — which makes sense, since the model is currently claiming disputes happen half the time.
lncaprat gets -8.7, firmly negative and by far the largest entry. In this slice the capability ratios are much larger in the rows the model over-predicted (mean 3.35) than in the rows it under-predicted (mean 0.67). Big values of the covariate line up with negative mistakes, so the coefficient should come down.
border gets 1, positive. Both bordering dyads in the slice had a dispute, and both are rows the model under-predicted, so the column has nothing pulling the other way. Raise it.
deml gets -3. The disputes here sit in dyads with lower democracy scores, so the covariate and the mistakes line up in opposite directions — a fact about ten rows, not a finding about world politics.

Four numbers, one per coefficient, each answering the same question the picture answered: from where we are standing, which way should this coefficient move? That is the whole content of a first derivative.
The clean \(X'(y-\pi)\) is a property of the logit, not a law of maximum likelihood. Every binary model’s score is a weighted sum of \((y_i - \text{fitted})\); the logistic link happens to make that weight exactly one. The probit’s does not. Where that weight comes from is worked out in the MLE estimator notes.

title: Likelihood Theory & Estimation Mechanics
section: The Hessian and information: how much the data actually tell us
text:
The Hessian and information: how much the data actually tell us
The second derivative of the log-likelihood at \(\beta\) is called the Hessian. It counts how much each observation tells us about \(\beta\); adding that up over the sample is what produces the standard errors. It measures the curvature of the function at \(\beta\) - it measures information, and indicates precision.
The Hessian, \(H(\beta)\) is the rate at which the slope itself changes, which is the curvature of the hill at the point we’re standing on - the log-likelihood value on the function associated with the values of \(\beta\) we guessed. There is a curvature for every pair of coefficients, so it is a \(k \times k\) matrix, not a vector. For the logit it works out to
\[
H(\beta) = -\sum_{i=1}^{n}\pi_i(1-\pi_i)\,x_i'x_i \;=\; -X'WX,
\qquad W = \mathrm{diag}\big(\pi_i(1-\pi_i)\big).
\]
That sum explains the word information. Each observation contributes one term: its covariates (\(x_i'x_i\)) scaled by the weight \(\pi_i(1-\pi_i)\). You should note that \(\pi_i(1-\pi_i)\) is the variance of the binomial, so we’re weighting by variances. Two things determine how much curvature the sample delivers:

How much the covariates move. A column that barely varies contributes almost nothing to \(x_i'x_i\), and a column that doesn’t vary at all contributes nothing whatsoever — there is no information about a coefficient in a variable that never changes.
How uncertain the model is about each row. The weight \(\pi_i(1-\pi_i)\) is largest — \(0.25\) — when \(\pi_i = 0.5\), and it falls toward zero as \(\pi_i\) approaches either 0 or 1. A row the model already calls at \(\pi = 0.99\) contributes essentially nothing: it is telling us what we already know. The rows that teach us about \(\beta\) are the ones the model finds hard to call.

Because the terms add over observations, information accumulates with the sample: more rows, more curvature, sharper hill. That is the mechanical reason big samples give small standard errors.
If we take the negative of this matrix, \(-H = X'WX\), the result is called the information matrix. It is a running total of how the sample informs us about \(\beta\).
If \(-H\) measures how much we know, then its inverse measures how much we don’t — and that is the variance of the guess at \(\beta\). It’s important to understand the second derivative (Hessian) provides these measures of uncertainty.
Figure 5 draws the weight — the second ingredient — and then shows where the dispute data actually sit on it.2


code
# How much does one observation contribute to the information? The weight
# pi*(1-pi) peaks at pi = .5 and vanishes at either extreme. The rug shows the
# fitted probabilities from the real dispute logit -- disputes are rare, so
# nearly every row sits in the low-weight corner on the left.

m_full <- glm(dispute ~ lncaprat + border + deml, family = binomial, data = dp)
pi_i   <- fitted(m_full)
w_i    <- pi_i * (1 - pi_i)

curve_d <- tibble(p = seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 400), w = p * (1 - p))

p_w <- ggplot(curve_d, aes(p, w)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, color = bu_green) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dotted", color = bu_black) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.295, size = 3.4, color = bu_black,
           label = "a coin-flip row carries the most: 0.25") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.99, y = 0.012, size = 3.4, color = bu_black, hjust = 1,
           label = "a near-certain row carries almost nothing") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.32)) +
  labs(title = "What one observation contributes",
       subtitle = expression("the weight " ~ pi[i](1 - pi[i]) ~ " in " ~ X*minute*W*X),
       x = expression("fitted probability," ~ pi[i]), y = "weight") +
  theme_minimal()

p_rug <- ggplot(tibble(p = pi_i), aes(p)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = bu_lightgreen, color = NA) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dotted", color = bu_black) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.20, y = Inf, vjust = 1.8, hjust = 0, size = 3.4, color = bu_black,
           label = "almost every dyad-year is\na near-certain zero") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Where the dispute data actually sit",
       subtitle = "fitted probabilities from the three-covariate logit",
       x = expression("fitted probability," ~ pi[i]), y = "dyad-years") +
  theme_minimal()

p_w + p_rug








Figure 5





Together the panels show a fact the sample size conceals. There are 20,990 dyad-years in dp, but disputes are rare, so nearly every row is one the model calls a near-certain zero and contributes almost no weight. The weights sum to 875.6, against the 5,248 we would have if every row were a coin flip — under a fifth of the curvature the row count advertises. The sample is large; the information in it is a good deal smaller than large. More on this when we get to rare events.
The second derivative does not lend itself to that kind of picture — there is no tangent to draw, and the useful thing about it is not its shape but its sign and its size. Take the sign first. It is negative everywhere on this likelihood, which is what guarantees the flat spot the score finds is a peak rather than a trough, and that there is only one of them. (If it went positive somewhere, the score could cross zero more than once and “set the derivative to zero” would stop identifying a unique answer. For the binomial it cannot happen.) The size is what the rest of this section is about, and Figure 5 is the closest thing to a picture of it: not the second derivative itself, but the per-observation weight that the sum in \(-X'WX\) is built from.
That the weights are strictly positive is what makes this true in general: it makes \(X'WX\) positive definite and \(H\) negative definite everywhere, so there is one hill, one top, and no false summits. Note the qualifier above — when it exists. There are data configurations for which no top exists at all, and we take those up later in the term.
One last thing to know about the Hessian - it is the source of every standard error in the model:
\[
\widehat{\text{SE}}(\widehat\beta) = \sqrt{\text{diag}\big[(-H)^{-1}\big]} = \sqrt{\text{diag}\big[(X'WX)^{-1}\big]},
\]
the square roots of the diagonal of the negated, inverted Hessian. Nothing new has to be computed and no extra assumption gets made; the uncertainty was already sitting inside the curvature. The next section is about why that is so, and what it means.






Take away




The score \(\nabla\ell(\beta)\) is the slope of the log-likelihood, one entry per coefficient. Each entry is the leftover association between one covariate and what the model is currently getting wrong.
Setting the score to zero says there is nothing left in any column of \(X\) that the model hasn’t used — the same condition OLS imposes with \(X'e = 0\).
The Hessian measures curvature, a \(k \times k\) matrix because there is a curvature for every pair of coefficients. Negate it and it is the information matrix: it measures how much this sample has to say about \(\beta\).
Information accumulates over observations, and each observation’s contribution is weighted by \(\pi_i(1-\pi_i)\). Rows the model already calls confidently teach us almost nothing; the informative rows are the ones it can’t call.
These two derivatives are what any numerical method, Newton–Raphson included, runs on — and they also stand on their own: between them they say where the estimate is and how much to trust it.

title: Likelihood Theory & Estimation Mechanics
section: Where the update rule comes from
text:
Where the update rule comes from
With both derivatives in hand we can say where the rule from Section 6 came from. This is where students most often get stuck, reasonably: we keep saying the goal is to make \(\ell(\beta)\) as large as possible, and the update rule doesn’t appear to contain \(\ell(\beta)\) anywhere. So what is Newton–Raphson doing to our log-likelihood?
Newton–Raphson is not a maximizer. It is a root-finder — a method for solving \(g(x) = 0\). Given a function and a starting guess, it tells you where that function crosses zero, by repeatedly following the tangent line down to the axis:
\[
x^{(t+1)} = x^{(t)} - \frac{g(x^{(t)})}{g'(x^{(t)})}.
\]
We don’t want \(\ell(\beta) = 0\); that would be meaningless. But we do have a root-finding problem, handed to us by the derivation above: the maximum of \(\ell\) is where \(\nabla\ell(\beta) = 0\). That is the middle panel of Figure 6 — a curve, and we want its crossing. So:






The bridge: we don’t hand Newton the log-likelihood, we hand it the gradient



Maximizing \(\ell(\beta)\) and solving \(\nabla\ell(\beta) = 0\) are the same task. So we apply the root-finder one derivative up: set \(g = \nabla\ell\). And because Newton’s rule needs the derivative of whatever it’s solving, \(g'\) becomes the derivative of the gradient — which is the Hessian, \(H\).
\[
\underbrace{x^{(t+1)} = x^{(t)} - \frac{g(x^{(t)})}{g'(x^{(t)})}}_{\text{Newton, for any root}}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\underbrace{\beta^{(t+1)} = \beta^{(t)} - H(\beta^{(t)})^{-1}\,\nabla\ell(\beta^{(t)})}_{\text{Newton, applied to } \nabla\ell = 0}
\]
That is why the Hessian shows up in an algorithm about maximization. It isn’t an optional refinement for taking better steps — it is simply \(g'\), the derivative Newton’s rule demands, for the particular \(g\) we chose.


Now substitute the two objects we just derived — the gradient and the Hessian of the binomial log-likelihood — and watch the update rule assemble itself:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla\ell(\beta) &= X'(y - \pi) &&\text{(the score: the gradient of } \ell) \\[4pt]
H(\beta) &= -X'WX &&\text{(the Hessian: the derivative of } \nabla\ell) \\[8pt]
\beta^{(t+1)} &= \beta^{(t)} - H^{-1}\nabla\ell
   \;=\; \beta^{(t)} - \big(-X'WX\big)^{-1}X'(y-\pi) \\[4pt]
  &= \beta^{(t)} + (X'WX)^{-1}X'(y - \pi).
\end{aligned}
\]
The two minus signs cancel — one from Newton’s rule, one from the Hessian being negative — which is why the update adds the step. And every symbol on that last line traces back to \(\ell(\beta)\): \(\pi\) is \(F(x\beta)\) from inside it, \(\nabla\ell\) is its first derivative, \(W\) collects the second. The log-likelihood isn’t absent from the update rule; it is the only thing in it.
The chain: write \(\ell\) → differentiate → set \(\nabla\ell = 0\) → hand it to a root-finder → the root-finder needs \(H\) → iterate. And since \(\nabla\ell = 0\) has no closed-form solution once there are \(x\) variables, the iterating is not optional.

title: Likelihood Theory & Estimation Mechanics
text:
Which way, and how far
That’s where the rule comes from; now what does it mean? The intuition is the hill-climber’s. The gradient tells us which way is up. The Hessian tells us how sharply the slope is changing, and therefore how far to go without sailing over the top: sharply curved, step conservatively; nearly flat, step boldly. Newton–Raphson packages both into
\[
\beta^{(t+1)} = \beta^{(t)} + \underbrace{(X'WX)^{-1}}_{\text{how far}}\underbrace{X'(y-\pi)}_{\text{which way}},
\]
and iterates until the score is essentially zero. Read the pieces as labeled: the gradient points uphill, the inverse Hessian scales the stride.
Why does curvature get a vote in how far we go? Figure 7 shows two hills with an identical slope at the current guess — so the score alone prescribes the same move on both — where the right answer is very different.


code
# Same slope at the starting point, different curvature. The score says "go
# right" in both panels and says it equally loudly. Only the second derivative
# knows that the sharp hill's top is close and the flat hill's top is far.

peak  <- 4
slope <- 3

one_hill <- function(a, ttl, sub, col) {
  start <- peak - slope / (2 * a)                 # point where the slope equals `slope`
  step  <- slope / (2 * a)                        # the Newton step from there
  g     <- seq(peak - 6, peak + 6, length.out = 400)
  d     <- tibble(b = g, y = -a * (g - peak)^2)
  tg    <- tibble(b = g, y = -a * (start - peak)^2 + slope * (g - start))

  ggplot(d, aes(b, y)) +
    geom_line(data = tg, aes(b, y), color = bu_grey, linewidth = 0.7) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, color = col) +
    geom_point(x = start, y = -a * (start - peak)^2, size = 3, color = bu_black) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = peak, linetype = "dotted", color = bu_black) +
    annotate("segment", x = start, xend = start + step, y = -34, yend = -34,
             arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm"), type = "closed"), color = bu_black) +
    annotate("text", x = start + step / 2, y = -34, vjust = -0.7, size = 3.4,
             color = bu_black, label = paste0("step = ", round(step, 2))) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(peak - 6, peak + 4), ylim = c(-38, 3)) +
    labs(title = ttl, subtitle = sub, x = expression(beta), y = "log-likelihood") +
    theme_minimal()
}

one_hill(2.0, "Sharp hill: step small",
         "steep curvature -- the top is close, so don't overshoot", bu_green) +
one_hill(0.3, "Flat hill: step big",
         "gentle curvature -- the top is far, so cover ground", bu_lightgreen)








Figure 7





The grey tangent has the same slope in both panels, so the gradient says the same thing in both — and says nothing about distance. What separates them is the second derivative. On the sharp hill the slope falls away fast, so the peak is near and a large step would sail over it. On the flat hill the slope barely changes, so the peak is far and a timid step wastes the trip. That is the work \((X'WX)^{-1}\) does: it converts “which way” into “how far.”
One more thing from the Hessian. Once the climb finishes, the standard errors are
\[
\widehat{\text{SE}}(\widehat\beta) = \sqrt{\text{diag}\big[(X'WX)^{-1}\big]} = \sqrt{\text{diag}\big[(-H)^{-1}\big]},
\]
— the square roots of the diagonal of the inverted Hessian. So the object we brought in to decide how far to step is also the source of every standard error in the model. The next section says why.






Take away




The score \(\nabla\ell(\beta)\) is the slope of the log-likelihood, one entry per coefficient. Each entry is the leftover association between one covariate and what the model is currently getting wrong.
Setting the score to zero says there is nothing left in any column of \(X\) that the model hasn’t used — the same condition OLS imposes with \(X'e = 0\).
The Hessian is curvature. Negate it and it is the information matrix, and the name is literal: it measures how much this sample has to say about \(\beta\).
Information accumulates over observations, and each observation’s contribution is weighted by \(\pi_i(1-\pi_i)\). Rows the model already calls confidently teach us almost nothing; the informative rows are the ones it can’t call.
Newton–Raphson is not a maximizer. It is a root-finder pointed at \(\nabla\ell = 0\), which is why the Hessian appears in it at all — it is the derivative the root-finder demands.
Read the update rule in two halves: the gradient says which way, the inverse Hessian says how far.

title: Likelihood Theory & Estimation Mechanics
text:
Analytic methods, and closed-form solutions
Take the binomial with no \(x\) variables at all. Every observation shares the same probability \(\pi\) — there is one unknown, a single number, and we want the value of it that makes our observed string of zeros and ones most probable. Write the log-likelihood, differentiate with respect to \(\pi\), set it to zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell(\pi) &= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big[\, y_i\log\pi + (1-y_i)\log(1-\pi)\,\big] \\[4pt]
          &= \Big(\textstyle\sum_i y_i\Big)\log\pi \;+\; \Big(n - \textstyle\sum_i y_i\Big)\log(1-\pi) \\[4pt]
\frac{d\ell}{d\pi} &= \frac{\sum_i y_i}{\pi} \;-\; \frac{n - \sum_i y_i}{1-\pi} \;=\; 0 \\[4pt]
(1-\pi)\textstyle\sum_i y_i &= \pi\Big(n - \textstyle\sum_i y_i\Big) \\[4pt]
\textstyle\sum_i y_i &= \pi\, n \\[4pt]
\widehat\pi &= \bbox[#A7DA92, 3pt, border: 1px solid #005A43]{\;\frac{\sum_i y_i}{n} \;=\; \bar y\;}
\end{aligned}
\]
The second line just counts: \(\sum_i y_i\) observations contribute a \(\log\pi\), the remaining \(n - \sum_i y_i\) contribute a \(\log(1-\pi)\). Two steps of algebra from there, and the answer is the sample mean of \(y\). No software, no starting value, no algorithm — a formula.
On the dispute data, that formula says the maximum likelihood estimate of \(\pi\) is the observed dispute rate:


code
dp <- read_dta(here::here("data", "dp.dta"))
dp$lncaprat <- log(dp$caprat)   # a capability ratio is multiplicative, so model it on the log scale

round(mean(dp$dispute), 4)


[1] 0.0451


Two names for what we just did, because you will meet both constantly. Solving a model by taking a derivative, setting it to zero, and rearranging is an analytic method — algebra and calculus. When an analytic method works, what it produces is a closed-form solution: an explicit formula for the estimate in terms of the data, like \(\widehat\pi = \bar y\). No starting values, no iteration, just straightforward computation.
Figure 3 draws the log-likelihood this formula maximizes, with the closed-form answer marked on it; it uses the democratic peace \(y\) variable, presence or absence of a dispute.


code
# The log-likelihood over its one unknown, with the value the algebra produced
# marked. I plot RELATIVE log-likelihood (subtracting the maximum) because the
# level carries no information -- only comparisons across values of pi do.

pi_hat <- mean(dp$dispute)
g_pi   <- seq(0.030, 0.070, length.out = 400)
ll_pi  <- sum(dp$dispute) * log(g_pi) + sum(1 - dp$dispute) * log(1 - g_pi)

ggplot(tibble(pi = g_pi, rel = ll_pi - max(ll_pi)), aes(pi, rel)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = bu_green) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = pi_hat, linetype = "dashed", color = bu_black) +
  annotate("text", x = pi_hat, y = -95, hjust = -0.1, size = 3.6, color = bu_black,
           label = paste0("hat(pi) == ", round(pi_hat, 4)), parse = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "Bernoulli: militarized disputes",
       subtitle = expression(hat(pi) == bar(y) ~ ", the sample proportion, found by algebra"),
       x = expression(pi), y = "relative log-likelihood") +
  theme_minimal()








Figure 3





One smooth hill with a single top: that shape is the structural fact that lets the calculus work. And hold onto its width. This hill is built on nearly 21,000 dyad-years, and by the end of these notes the width of a log-likelihood at its top will be the standard error.
If maximum likelihood always went like this, it would be a footnote in a calculus course rather than a semester-long class. It doesn’t, and it’s worth being precise about where it falls apart.

Where the analytic method fails
We don’t actually want a single \(\pi\) for the whole sample. We want it to vary with covariates; that is the entire point of a regression. So we parameterize — \(\pi_i = \Lambda(x_i\beta)\) — and differentiate again, now with respect to \(\beta\) rather than \(\pi\).
Put the two derivatives we built earlier side by side, the binomial’s and the Normal’s, and set each to zero. They are as close to identical as two expressions can be:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{binomial:}\quad
  \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \beta} &= X'\big(y - \Lambda(X\beta)\big) \;=\; 0 \\[8pt]
\text{Normal:}\quad
  \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \beta} &= X'\big(y - X\beta\big) \;=\; 0
\end{aligned}
\]
Same \(X'\), same \(y\), same “observed minus fitted” in the middle. The only difference is the four characters wrapped around \(X\beta\) on the top line — and that difference decides everything.
On the bottom line, \(\beta\) sits out in the open, multiplied by matrices we already know. Distribute, collect, invert, and it comes free: \(X'y = X'X\beta\), so \(\widehat\beta = (X'X)^{-1}X'y\). We did exactly this a few pages ago, and the answer was OLS.
On the top line, try the same moves. Distribute the \(X'\) and you get \(X'y = X'\Lambda(X\beta)\) — and then you are stuck, because there is no way to peel \(\Lambda\) off the right-hand side and leave \(\beta\) standing alone. It is inside a nonlinear function, wrapped up with the data, and no rearranging extracts it. The same is true of the Poisson’s \(X'(y - e^{X\beta})\). There is no closed form. Not one we have failed to find — one that does not exist.
What we use instead is a numerical method: a procedure that searches for the answer by evaluating the function over and over, rather than solving for it. Guess a \(\beta\), see what the function says, use that to make a better guess, repeat until you stop improving. The particular numerical method this course uses is Newton–Raphson; we’ll build it in the maximization notes.
To prepare for the Newton-Raphson, let’s assemble two things Newton–Raphson needs — the first and second derivatives of the log-likelihood — and show what they tell us about the estimate quite apart from any algorithm.






Take away




Writing down a log-likelihood and solving it are two different jobs. The first recipe always works the same way; the second is where models differ in difficulty.
An analytic method — differentiate, set to zero, rearrange — gives a closed-form solution when it works: an explicit formula, like \(\widehat\pi = \bar y\). No starting values, no iteration.
Add covariates and it stops working. \(\beta\) ends up buried inside a nonlinear link, \(\Lambda(x\beta)\), and no rearranging gets it out.
The linear model is the exception, and it is worth knowing exactly why: its link is the identity, so \(\beta\) sits out in the open and one line of algebra frees it.
We use a numerical method instead: search rather than solve.

title: Likelihood Theory & Estimation Mechanics
text:
The first derivative (score, gradient)
The first derivative of the log-likelihood goes by two names we use interchangeably — the score, or the gradient — written \(\nabla\ell(\beta)\) either way.
The log-likelihood assigns one number to every candidate value of \(\beta\): how probable this sample is under it. The score asks a question about that number, one coefficient at a time — nudge this coefficient up a hair, holding the others still; does the sample get more probable or less? One answer per coefficient, so the score is a \(k \times 1\) vector. Positive says raise it, negative says lower it, and when every entry is zero at once — no nudge to anything helps — we are on top of the hill.
For the logit, the score is:
\[
\nabla\ell(\beta) \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \pi_i)\,x_i' \;=\; X'(y - \pi).
\]
This should look familiar. \((y - \pi)\) is the model’s mistakes, one per row; multiplying by \(X'\) runs each covariate’s column against those mistakes and sums, one number per covariate. So:

each element of the score is the leftover association between one covariate and what the model is currently getting wrong.

Say the model systematically under-predicts disputes in bordering dyads. Then the mistakes are positive in exactly the rows where border is 1, their products are positive, and the border score comes out positive: this coefficient is too small, and that column still has unused information in it.
Think of finding the maximum the same way. Setting \(\nabla\ell(\beta) = 0\) says there is no leftover association between any covariate and the mistakes — every column of \(X\) is used up.
Let’s see that at work. Figure 4 stands at three candidate values of \(\beta_0\) — one too low, one too high, one right — and reads the first derivative at each.


code
# What a single guess tells you. Three candidate values of beta-0 on the
# intercept-only dispute hill: one too low, one too high, one right. At each we
# read the FIRST derivative and ask what it says about where the maximum is.
sy <- sum(dp$dispute); nn <- nrow(dp)
ll0   <- function(b) sy * log(plogis(b)) + (nn - sy) * log(1 - plogis(b))
d1_0  <- function(b) sy - nn * plogis(b)                 # score
d2_0  <- function(b) -nn * plogis(b) * (1 - plogis(b))   # Hessian
b_mle <- qlogis(mean(dp$dispute))

guess <- tibble(b = c(-4.0, b_mle, -2.2),
                lab = c("guess too low", "the answer", "guess too high")) %>%
  mutate(ll = ll0(b), score = d1_0(b))

gb   <- seq(-4.6, -1.8, length.out = 400)
hill <- tibble(b = gb, ll = ll0(gb), score = d1_0(gb))

# short tangent at each guess, so the slope is visible ON the curve
tang <- guess %>% rowwise() %>%
  do(tibble(b = .$b + c(-0.32, 0.32), lab = .$lab,
            y = ll0(.$b) + d1_0(.$b) * c(-0.32, 0.32))) %>% ungroup()

p_top <- ggplot(hill, aes(b, ll)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, color = bu_green) +
  geom_line(data = tang, aes(b, y, group = lab), color = bu_black,
            linewidth = 0.9, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_point(data = guess, aes(b, ll), size = 3, color = bu_lightgreen) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = b_mle, linetype = "dashed", color = bu_grey) +
  annotate("text", x = -4.05, y = ll0(-4.0), hjust = 1.05, vjust = 1.9, size = 3.2,
           color = bu_black, label = "guess too low:\nstill climbing") +
  annotate("text", x = b_mle, y = ll0(b_mle), vjust = -0.9, size = 3.2,
           color = bu_black, label = "the answer: flat") +
  annotate("text", x = -2.35, y = ll0(-2.2), hjust = 1, vjust = 2.4, size = 3.2,
           color = bu_black, label = "guess too high:\nalready falling") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(min(hill$ll), max(hill$ll) + 190)) +
  labs(title = "Stand at a guess and look at the slope",
       subtitle = "dotted lines are the tangent -- the first derivative -- at three candidate values",
       x = NULL, y = "log-likelihood") +
  theme_minimal()

p_bot <- ggplot(hill, aes(b, score)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = bu_black, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, color = bu_lightgreen) +
  geom_point(data = guess, aes(b, score), size = 3, color = bu_green) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = b_mle, linetype = "dashed", color = bu_grey) +
  geom_segment(data = guess %>% filter(lab != "the answer"),
               aes(x = b, xend = b, y = 0, yend = score),
               color = bu_grey, linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = -4.0, y = d1_0(-4.0), vjust = -1.0, size = 3.2, color = bu_black,
           label = "score > 0: the answer is to the RIGHT") +
  annotate("text", x = -2.2, y = d1_0(-2.2), vjust = 1.9, size = 3.2, color = bu_black,
           label = "score < 0: the answer is to the LEFT") +
  annotate("text", x = b_mle, y = 0, vjust = -1.2, hjust = -0.05, size = 3.2,
           color = bu_black, label = "score = 0: stop") +
  labs(title = "Read that slope as a number: the score",
       subtitle = "what matters here is where the curve CROSSES zero, not the curve's own slope",
       x = expression("intercept," ~ beta[0]), y = "score (first derivative)") +
  theme_minimal()

p_top / p_bot








Figure 4





In the top panel we stand at each of the three guesses and look at the slope of the hill underneath us — the dotted tangent lines. At \(\beta_0 = -4\) the hill is still rising, so the answer is further right. At \(-2.2\) it is falling, so we have gone past and the answer is back to the left. At the dashed line the tangent is flat, and there is no direction left that improves anything, so we’re at a flat point, hopefully a maximum.
The bottom panel is the same first derivative but presented as a number rather than a tangent line: this is the score at each of the three values of \(\beta\). This is a plot of the first derivatives, NOT of the likelihood (compare the y-axes in the two panels). What matters in the bottom panel is where the curve crosses zero, not whether the curve itself looks flat. The score is a steeply sloping line through most of this range — that’s fine and expected, since the slope of the hill really is changing fast. The estimate is the single place the score’s value hits zero. A positive score says the maximum is to the right; a negative score says it is to the left; a zero score says stop.
